comments: Which spoken phrases work which DCS cockpit control.
The 'control' field is a DCS control NAME, not a key, and must match DCS's own
spelling exactly - 'Navigation lights' has a lowercase L, 'Airbrake' is one word.
The keys come from DCS's binding files, so if you rebind a control in the game's
options this file needs no change: press 'Re-read bindings' in the manager.
A control your aircraft does not have is simply absent from its bindings, and the
command refuses itself. Nothing here needs to be per-aircraft.
Edit the 'phrases' lists to change what you say, then stop and start listening so
the recogniser rebuilds its grammar.
'requires' is checked against what the mission publishes. onGround==0 means
airborne, onGround==1 means on the ground.
Destructive controls - eject, jettison, engine shutdown, weapons release, master
arm, countermeasures - are refused in code even if named here.
Some controls are toggles rather than explicit up/down, because that is all DCS
exposes a literal key for. A toggle is only safe where you can see the result:
flaps and canopy you can, which is why they are toggles and the gear is not.
A note on 'airbrake on' / 'airbrake off': those two phrasings are one word apart
with opposite effects, and were never measured. 'out' / 'in' are phonetically
further apart and are the safer pair. If the recogniser ever confuses on and off,
delete those two phrases - nothing else depends on them. To check first:
python tools/phrase_separability.py "airbrake on" "airbrake off"
The gear phrases were measured across twenty utterances with zero confusions.

cockpit_gear_up.refusal: not while you're on the ground

cockpit_flaps.refusal: this aircraft has no flaps binding

cockpit_canopy.refusal: not in flight - the canopy would not survive it
